role: Property Project Manager for a Large Residential Community
headline: Fourteen years up from estate steward, just put in charge of an old residential community in Beijing's Changping district with more than forty buildings and over ten thousand households: a property project manager with twenty-odd residents' group chats on the phone, who has every building's radiators pressure-tested before the heating season
unit: The property service center of a property management company at a large residential community in Changping, Beijing
unit_type: Private property management company (dozens of projects in Beijing), about 150 staff on this project
education: Junior college diploma in property management
level: Work orders, fee collection, fire safety, heating, elevator maintenance, the owners' committee: you've handled every one, and you spent three years as project manager of a two-thousand-household estate. But in this old community of over ten thousand households, with aging buildings, aging pipes and twenty-odd group chats, you are still learning it building by building.
intro: You studied property management in Beijing and started out after graduation as an estate steward. Fourteen years in the trade, three of them as project manager of a two-thousand-household estate. This year the company moved you to this old community in Changping with over ten thousand households. The property service center is in a ground-floor shopfront under one of the buildings, and every morning there's a line at the door of people reporting repairs. As of today you are in charge of the heating, elevators, parking and quarrels of more than forty buildings, learning to catch every small thing in a community bigger than many county towns.
salary_note: Estimate: property project managers at large Beijing communities earn above the national average, with year-end bonuses tied to the fee collection rate and the complaint rate. In years when an old community's fees are low and hard to collect, the bonus shrinks.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Handling emergencies and residents' urgent troubles

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Taking repair calls, dispatching work orders and following up

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 23 related listings nationwide, 1 in this city (the job database is mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: You take the first metro from your rented place in Huilongguan and buy a jianbing crepe at the breakfast stall by the community gate, reading your phone as you eat: overnight, the residents' group chats gained more than a hundred messages.

Morning meeting. The engineering supervisor says the radiators in Building 12 lost pressure in last week's test. The customer service supervisor reads yesterday's work orders: seven leaks, two elevators, three noise complaints, and someone running an extension cord down a stairwell to charge an e-bike.

You take the engineering supervisor to Building 12 and knock on door after door to check the radiators. On the seventh floor a resident swapped a valve himself and didn't seal it properly. You note it and have a repairman fix it before the day is out.

The director of the residents' committee calls: next week the district is coming to inspect garbage sorting, and the bin stations need someone on duty. You work through the cleaning staff and move two people over from landscaping.

An elderly resident on a cane comes to the service center: the dog upstairs barks at night and she can't sleep. You pour her a glass of water and listen for half an hour, then go upstairs and knock. A young man answers and says the dog was only just adopted and is afraid of strangers.

In the office you check this month's fee collection rate: three points below the same time last year. Residents in a few buildings say the elevators are always broken and they won't pay. You pull up the maintenance records for those buildings' elevators.

The owners' committee meets to discuss repainting the surface parking. You bring the site plan; the seven members propose three options. You write them down and say that next week you'll bring one that fits more cars without blocking the fire lanes.
On the last metro home you answer thirty-odd messages from residents. The last one: the light in Building 6, Entrance 3, is out. Fixed first thing tomorrow.

ladder.title: Estate Steward
ladder.focus: Look after the residents of two or three buildings: take repair requests, chase fees, walk the buildings, post notices and answer messages in the group chats. You move up by remembering people and getting things done.

ladder.title: Customer Service Supervisor / Assistant Project Manager
ladder.focus: Lead a customer service team handling work orders, complaints, fees and community events, and deal with the owners' committee and the residents' committee on the project manager's behalf.

ladder.title: Property Project Manager
ladder.focus: Run everything on a project: engineering, security, cleaning and landscaping, customer service, fees and budget, answering to residents, the owners' committee, the subdistrict office and the company.

ladder.title: Regional Manager
ladder.focus: Run a region of several to a dozen-odd projects, set budgets and staffing, bid for new projects, and handle the hardest problems on each one.

ladder.title: City Company General Manager
ladder.focus: Run all of the company's projects in Beijing and thousands of staff, set business targets, expand into new business, and deal with developers, government departments and group headquarters.

ai_tasks.name: Taking repair calls, dispatching work orders and following up
ai_tasks.how: An AI service agent can take calls, answer common questions in the group chats, dispatch orders by type, chase progress and run satisfaction follow-ups. A person only spot-checks the dispatching and handles what it can't answer.

ai_tasks.name: Maintaining buildings, water, power, gas, heating and fire systems, and organizing repairs
ai_tasks.how: AI can schedule inspections from repair records and equipment data, warn of failures and track progress. Going to look, doing the repair, and dealing face to face with the water, power and heating utilities still takes people and a repair crew.

ai_tasks.name: Organizing security and safety patrols
ai_tasks.how: AI can watch the cameras, spot clutter in stairwells and e-bikes charged on extension cords, and draw up rosters. How a guard talks someone down on the spot, how to handle it, and who answers if something happens is only for people.

ai_tasks.name: Organizing cleaning, landscaping and community events
ai_tasks.how: AI can plan cleaning and landscaping, check work records and draft event plans and notices. Sweeping and tending take people, and whether an event comes together and residents want to come depends on someone going out and making it happen.

ai_tasks.name: Planning the use of shared spaces and facilities
ai_tasks.how: AI can survey current conditions, look up how similar estates do it, work out income and costs and draft a plan. How parking is marked out and what to do with an empty lot, and whether residents will accept it, takes a person to ask, negotiate and decide.

ai_tasks.name: Handling emergencies and residents' urgent troubles
ai_tasks.how: A flooded garage on a stormy night, people trapped in an elevator, an elderly resident living alone who can't be reached: a person has to be there to judge, direct and reassure, and to take responsibility.

ai_tasks.name: Talking face to face with residents, the owners' committee and the residents' committee
ai_tasks.how: Whether to raise fees, whether to add elevators, whose dog kept whom awake: someone has to sit down and talk it through household by household, and when it's done, someone signs.

events.e_heating: On November 15, the first day of heating, the service center phones rang from seven in the morning to ten at night: more than three hundred households said their radiators weren't warm. You led engineering building by building, bleeding air and checking valves, and a week later complaints were down to twenty-odd households.
events.e_rain: A July downpour sent water over the flood barrier at the garage entrance. You worked through the night with the guards and engineering, stacking sandbags and running pumps, calling car owners one by one to move their cars out of the garage. By dawn the water had gone down, and not one car was flooded.
events.e_elevator_trap: One evening an old elevator stopped between floors with an elderly woman and her grandson inside. While you got the maintenance company on its way, you talked to the boy through the door. Twenty minutes later it opened, and the boy ran out first and hugged you.
events.e_fee_drop: That year the fee collection rate fell below eighty percent, and the company singled out your project at the quarterly meeting. You went building by building to the residents who hadn't paid and heard hundreds of complaints. Half of them, you thought, were fair.
events.e_ai_service: The company brought in an AI service agent that takes repair calls and group chat questions first, dispatching and following up automatically. Customer service's load dropped by half, but going through the records you found it had marked a leak from upstairs as resolved because the repairman tapped complete.
events.e_ai_camera: The community installed AI cameras that automatically flag clutter in stairwells, e-bikes in elevators and extension-cord charging. In the first month they flagged more than four hundred times. You had security check each one: most were real, and a few dozen were quilts hung out to air in the stairwell.
events.e_old_alone: A steward said an elderly woman living alone in Building 18 hadn't come down for her milk in two days. You took people to knock and reached her daughter: the old woman had fallen and couldn't get up, and was taken to hospital. Her daughter later brought a silk banner of thanks, which you hung on the innermost wall of the service center.
events.e_snow: A heavy snow fell all night. At four in the morning you took the cleaners and guards out to the main road, sweeping, spreading de-icer and laying straw mats on the steps. When people left for work at seven, the road was clear.
events.e_catkin: In April willow catkins drifted all over the community, where one spark on the grass could burn a whole patch. You had people water every afternoon and reminded residents in the group chats again and again not to smoke downstairs. That season there wasn't a single fire.
events.e_fight: Two residents came to the service center fighting over a surface parking space: one said first come, first served; the other said he'd paid for it. You mediated for an hour, finally pulled the camera footage and payment records, and both left not entirely happy.
events.e_renovation: The community was put on the old estate renewal list: new pipes, repainted facades, repaired roads. That year you ran between the contractor, the subdistrict office and the residents every day, and the hardest part was deciding which building would lose water first, since every one wanted to go last.
events.e_lift: The first retrofitted elevator you helped coordinate was installed at Building 2, Entrance 3. The ground-floor resident was firmly against it at first, and you sat in his home seven times. The day it opened, he was the first to step in and press the button.
events.e_stomach: Years of mealtimes broken by phone calls and your stomach has started to hurt, and your checkup shows borderline high blood pressure too. The doctor told you to eat on time, and you keep a packet of soda crackers in your office drawer.
events.e_insult: A resident spent half the night cursing the management in a group chat, saying you take the money and do nothing, and posted your photo. The next day you went to his home: his bathroom had been leaking for two weeks and no one had come. You had a repairman fix it that day and explained nothing.
events.e_spring_fest: Before Spring Festival you held an event in the community square for writing couplets and making dumplings, and more than two hundred people came. A resident who was always the angriest in the group chats spent the afternoon beside you, folding dumplings.
events.e_family: Your child is in primary school back in Baoding, living with the grandparents, and you get back once a month. You've never been to a parent-teacher meeting. On the phone your child said: the teacher asked what my parents do, and I said they look after houses.
events.e_house: You finally bought an apartment in Yanjiao, adding an hour to the round trip each day. On moving day the first thing you did, without thinking, was check the pressure gauge on the stairwell fire hydrant.
events.e_tender: The owners' committee said it would put the property contract out to tender again, and several companies came to look at the project. You didn't go lobbying; you compiled these years' repair records, accounts and list of fixes into one binder and gave it to the committee. In the end your contract was renewed.
events.e_ai_budget: Now a project's work orders, inspections, energy use and fees all live in the system, and AI produces the monthly report and budget in half a day. The service center has half the customer service staff it had; those who stayed spend their days visiting, knocking on doors and sitting down to listen.
events.e_old_staff: Niu, a steward you trained, went to manage another project. Before she left she filled a notebook with every household in her three buildings: whose old parent has bad legs, whose dog is afraid of strangers.
events.e_charger: You had three hundred e-bike charging points installed in the community, and extension-cord charging dropped by more than half. While they went in, some said they took up too much space; in the first month after, there was a line at the chargers every day.

c_cost.title: The company wants labor costs cut
c_cost.situation: Fees haven't risen in years while labor costs rise every year, and the company wants your project to cut ten percent of its staff this year: a few fewer guard posts, a few fewer cleaners. Cutting protects the project's profit and your bonus; not cutting means finding another way to balance the books.

options.label: Cut as told
options.result: You merged several night guard posts and moved stairwell cleaning to every other day. The books balanced and your bonus was safe, but that half year, stairwell complaints doubled.

options.label: Hold the line and find another way
options.result: You repainted the surface parking to fit more than a hundred extra spaces and leased an empty shopfront to a community canteen, and the extra income just covered those posts. The company's general manager came to look once and never mentioned cuts again.

c_fee.title: Raise the property fee?
c_fee.situation: The community's fee hasn't changed in over ten years, the elevators and pipes are old, and there isn't enough money for repairs. Raising it takes a general meeting of owners and a majority vote, and you'd have to make the case building by building. Not raising it means fixing only the most urgent things and putting the rest off.

options.label: Push for the increase
options.result: You put every elevator's age and every pipe section's repair record into one table and presented it at the foot of every building. The vote failed by a few points, but afterward fewer people cursed the elevators in the group chats.

options.label: Hold off, fix the urgent things
options.result: Every year you spent the money on elevators and heating first and queued everything else. Residents said your management was stingy, but in winter the radiators were warm.

c_ai.title: Pilot smart property management across the project?
c_ai.situation: The company wants to pick one project to pilot smart property management: AI service agent, AI cameras, equipment monitoring, online payment, all of it. The pilot's project manager would spend most of a year setting rules and training staff and residents; complaints might rise in the meantime, and if it works, the credit goes to the company.

options.label: Take the pilot
options.result: You set one rule: any work order the AI marks resolved gets a home visit within a week. You also had stewards teach elderly residents to report repairs by phone at the service center every week. Six months later your project was the company's model.

options.label: Let another project go first
options.result: You said this community was too old and had too many elderly residents, and you'd wait for another project to find the way. A year later you brought in the system using their experience and avoided a few wrong turns.

c_lift.title: Lead the push for retrofitted elevators
c_lift.situation: More than forty old buildings in the community have no elevators, and more and more of the people on the fifth and sixth floors are elderly. Adding an elevator needs every household in an entrance to sign, and the ground floor often refuses. Property management isn't obliged to handle it, but the subdistrict office hopes you'll lead the coordination. It would cost you countless evenings.

options.label: Lead it
options.result: You held a coordination meeting at every entrance, working out light, noise and compensation for the ground-floor residents. The first year three elevators went in; by the third year, twenty.

options.label: Support it, don't lead it
options.result: You said management could support construction and maintenance, but residents should lead it themselves. A few went in, all pushed through by residents, and you helped with the paperwork.

c_commercial.title: Manage an office tower instead
c_commercial.situation: The company has taken on a Grade A office tower in the Chaoyang CBD and wants to move you there as project manager, at twenty percent more pay, dealing with corporate tenants: no more group chats, no more dogs barking at midnight. But it's different work, and the goodwill and know-how you've built up in housing would be no use.

options.label: Go to the office tower
options.result: In the tower you learned to answer tenants' emails in English, and the lobby flowers are changed every week. Now and then you still dream of those three hundred calls on the first day of heating.

options.label: Stay in the community
options.result: You said you'd only just got to know this community. That winter, heating complaints were less than half of what they were your first year.

c_region.title: Apply for Regional Manager
c_region.situation: The company is promoting a Regional Manager to run a dozen-odd projects across northern Beijing, set budgets and staffing, bid for new projects and take on the hardest problems at every one. You'd spend less time in any one community and more in meetings, on the road and at banquets.

options.label: Apply
options.result: At the interview you talked about the rainstorm and the binder of repair records you gave the owners' committee. The general manager asked how you'd make a dozen projects work like that. You said: have every project manager go knock on a door.

options.label: Stay with this community
options.result: You didn't apply. That year the community's fee collection rate got back to ninety percent. At the year-end meeting you said nothing, only wiped down the service center's wall of thank-you banners.

c_home.title: Go back to Baoding
c_home.situation: Your child is about to start middle school, and the grandparents aren't as strong as they were. A property company in Baoding wants you back to manage a new estate at half the pay, but you'd be home for dinner every night and could go to parent-teacher meetings.

options.label: Go back to Baoding
options.result: The day you left you handed over the twenty-odd group chats one by one, and before leaving each you wrote one line: for anything, ask the new manager. He's reliable.
options.end: Back in Baoding you manage a new estate: new buildings, fewer people, only three group chats. After school your child comes to the service center to do homework, and when you finish a call you turn around to go over the mistakes.

options.label: Stay in Beijing
options.result: You talked with your family on video a long time and decided to work a few more years. That weekend you went back to Baoding and attended your first parent-teacher meeting, sitting in the back row.

c_community.title: The subdistrict office wants you for community work
c_community.situation: After all these years dealing with the subdistrict and residents' committees, the subdistrict's community service center wants you to head its elder care services, running meal points and home visits across several communities. The pay is less than now, but you'd no longer have to deal with fees and profits.

options.label: Take the community service job
options.result: The day you left property management, you took a photo of the banner on the service center wall and left it hanging there.
options.end: You ran the meal points and home visits at the community service center for many years, watching elderly residents line up for lunch every noon. Sometimes, passing that old community, you look up and count which entrances got their elevators.

options.label: Stay in property management
options.result: You turned it down and recommended a steward you once trained. After she went, she sent you a photo of the meal point, with a menu she'd written by hand.

c_gm.title: Apply for City Company General Manager
c_gm.situation: The general manager of the Beijing city company is retiring, and the group wants a successor from among the regional managers to run more than sixty projects across the city and thousands of staff, set business targets, and negotiate new business with developers and government departments. You'd spend most of your time in meeting rooms and at banquet tables and get down to a garage only a few times a year.

options.label: Apply
options.result: Your application was only three pages, and the first was a photo: sandbags at the garage entrance that stormy night. The people from the group looked at it a long time and asked what it had to do with running a business. You said: whether owners renew depends on nights like that.

options.label: Keep your region
options.result: You said you'd rather stay close to the projects. That year not one project in your region was replaced by its owners' committee, and you took on three new ones.

endings.retire: On your last day you handed over the service center keys and the twenty-odd group chats to your successor and took one last walk around the community. The retrofitted elevators glowed at their entrances one after another, and the surface parking was marked in neat rows. The jianbing seller at the gate asked if you'd be back tomorrow. You said yes, for a jianbing.
endings.burnout: That year your stomach and blood pressure gave out together, and the doctor said you couldn't keep taking hundreds of calls a day. You quit, went back to Baoding and rested for a year, sitting by the Lotus Pond garden every day. Your phone stayed quiet for a long time, but you still woke at night thinking some building had sprung a leak.

stages: You run everything on a project: every morning engineering, security, cleaning and customer service report on the day before; in the afternoon you walk the buildings and take the hardest complaints; in the evening you meet the owners' committee. The collection rate, complaint rate, budget and fire inspections all weigh on you, and the calls from the subdistrict and residents' committees, the company's quarterly reviews and the group chats of ten thousand households all have to be caught by you.

You run a dozen-odd projects across northern Beijing: setting each one's budget and staffing, reviewing project managers' monthly reports, bidding for new projects, and negotiating contracts with developers, owners' committees and subdistrict offices. When a project's garage floods in a storm or a project is about to be replaced, you're the one who goes. You rarely walk buildings anymore, but at every project you still look first at the garage's flood barrier.

You run all the company's projects in Beijing: budgets and staffing for more than sixty estates and office towers and thousands of employees, the yearly business targets, and expansion into new business and new districts. You meet with developers' executives, district authorities and group headquarters, and sign the annual budget and major contracts. Every winter on the first day of heating, you still pick an old community and spend a morning at its service center listening to the phones.
work: A month before heating season you drew up a chart: all forty-odd buildings pressure-tested one by one, with who goes, which day, and whom to call if pressure drops, pinned to the engineering office wall. You crossed off each building as it was done.

A member of the owners' committee said in a meeting that the cleaners were slacking. You didn't argue; at six the next morning you walked the community with him and showed him how the cleaning women worked through building after building.

Before a fire inspection you walked every building's fire lanes with security, cleared dozens of e-bikes and a roomful of cardboard boxes out of three buildings, and knocked on door after door to tell residents why.

A project was about to be replaced by its owners' committee. You lived at that project for a week, knocking on doors with its project manager every day, and finally took a list of fixes to the committee.

Bidding to manage a new estate, a panel member asked why your price was higher. You said every one of our project managers pressure-tests the radiators personally, and laid the test chart on the table.

Setting the year-end budget, the company wanted every project in your region to cut ten percent of its staff. You worked through it project by project and in the end cut at two with new buildings and few residents, leaving the old communities untouched.

The group wanted profits up ten percent next year. You laid out the collection rates and repair backlogs of all sixty-odd projects and settled on five percent, writing the other five into an elevator replacement plan for three old communities.

A developer wanted to hand you the property management of a whole new district on condition that no fees were charged for the first three years. You worked the numbers all night and replied: we can charge less, but not nothing, or who fixes things in those three years?
You added one line to the evaluation of every project manager in the company: knock on at least twenty doors a month and write it down in a notebook, which you'll spot-check at year end.
past: In middle school in Baoding you lived in an old work-unit housing compound. The old man who kept the gate was the one everyone went to when a pipe froze or a child forgot the key.
Your gaokao (college entrance exam) score wasn't high, and you chose property management at a vocational college in Beijing. Your mother said at least it's in Beijing.

After graduating you joined this property company as a steward in charge of three buildings. In your first month chasing fees, doors were shut in your face more than a dozen times; by the second month you knew every household's surname.

You became customer service supervisor, leading six stewards. That winter the heating failed at one estate, and you answered phones at the service center for three days and lost your voice for a week.
You became assistant to a project manager, and at your first owners' committee meeting you watched how he settled one matter amid seven people arguing.
The company put you in charge of a two-thousand-household estate. In three years as project manager you raised the fee collection rate from eighty percent to ninety-five.

At a year-end company meeting, someone said the old Changping community with over ten thousand households needed a project manager; the last two hadn't lasted a year. You thought about it all night, and the next day you put your name forward.

late.pension_note: Estimate: private property companies in Beijing mostly pay pension contributions on the lower-middle range of wages, with no enterprise annuity, so after retirement the basic pension is about forty percent of your last monthly salary.
scenes: Your first month of retirement, you still wake at seven and reach for your phone to check the group chats, before remembering you've left them all.

The company asked you back to give new project managers a lesson, and you talked about the first day of heating. Afterward a young person asked whether you still need to answer calls like that now there's an AI service agent. You said yes: what you're answering is people.

At your own estate the owners' committee was being re-elected, and the neighbors put you forward. At your first meeting you asked for the management company's repair records and went through them page by page.

Your grandchild asked what you used to do. You thought a moment and said: looked after the heating and the quarrels of ten thousand households. He said you must have been amazing. You said: it was all right.
In the early days after you stopped, you sat by the Lotus Pond in Baoding every morning with your phone left at home, and slowly your stomach stopped hurting.
A few times you stood in for the old gatekeeper at your family's compound, and when someone's pipe froze, you went with a wrench.
On the day you filed your retirement papers you took a bus to Beijing. The jianbing stall at that community's gate was still there; you bought one and ate it standing outside the service center.
In your first year on a different path, whenever you walked into an estate you still checked first whether the stairwell was cluttered and the fire hydrant door shut.
On the street you ran into the ground-floor resident who had opposed the elevator. Carrying groceries, he said he takes the elevator now too; his legs aren't what they were.
Niu, the steward you once trained, became a regional manager and sent you a photo: on her desk, too, a handwritten notebook about the households.
November 15 came around again and the heating came on. You put your hand on the radiator: warm. You remembered those three hundred calls and smiled.

In a cupboard you found the old notebook, page after page of building, entrance, household: swapped his own valve, old mother with bad legs, dog afraid of strangers. The ink had faded a little, and you looked at it a long time.

closing.retire: Many years later, one winter night, you stood on your balcony watching the windows of the building opposite glow warm yellow, one after another. You knew behind every window ran a heating pipe that someone, some November, had pressure-tested.
closing.burnout: Many years later, one snowy morning, you opened the door to find someone had already swept a path across the courtyard and laid straw mats on the steps. You walked out along that path, and felt steady inside.
closing.end: Many years later, in a drawer, you found an old key from the service center, its tag reading: garage pump room. You held it in your hand and looked at it a while, then put it back.
